newsitem.title: UK: Dlr firm in Europe on NY Fed McDonough's remarks.
newsitem.headline: Dlr firm in Europe on NY Fed McDonough's remarks.

text.p: The dollar rose in late European trade, finding support from New York Federal Reserve President William McDonough's comments that a strong dollar was in the interests of the U.S.

The dollar briefly tested above key resistance at 1.7075 marks on the remarks but nervousness ahead of the French second round voting on Sunday and the ongoing asset revaluation row between Germany's central bank and the government put a lid on further dollar gains.
Dealers said trade was thin with most of activity in position squaring ahead of the weekend.

New York Fed's McDonough, speaking at the World Forex Conference in Toronto, said a strong dollar was in the interests of the U.S., as was a strong euro. He also said that second quarter information pointed to a slowing U.S. economy.
The dollar was firmer against the mark and yen but kept within recent range tops of 1.71 marks and 117 yen, said analysts.

"It would have been a lot higher if it had not been battered by dollar/yen's fallout recently," said Nick Parsons, forex strategist at Paribas in London. "The market is aware it's not a one-way bet and it's aware of change in G7 policy."
By 1540 GMT, dollar/mark was trading at 1.7078/83 against 1.6992/02 late Thursday in Europe. Dollar/yen stood at 116.36/46 from 116.14/24 yen.
There was little net reaction to the second estimate of U.S. first quarter GDP showing growth of 5.8 percent vs a previously released 5.6 percent. A 6.0 percent rate had been forecast.
U.S. April new home sales data came in below expectations at 772,000 but the March figure was revised upwards to 836,000, its strongest level in nearly 11 years.
The Chicago May purchasing managers index and the University of Michigan May consumer sentiment index had little impact.
Events in Europe continued to be the dominant theme for the dollar and market focus was on Sunday's French vote.

Growing expectations of a victory by France's opposition Socialists has raised the prospect of a broad-based start to Europe's monetary union and a softer euro, seen as positive for the dollar and negative for the mark.

Meantime, the row between the Bundesbank and the German government over Bonn's plans to revalue the central bank's assets continues to simmer. This outcome is far from clear and analysts are divided as to what the implications are for the currency markets.

"Germany could push the revaluation plan through which would likely see a soft EMU and weaker mark, but there is also a risk of the project being delayed which would mean a stronger mark," said Mark Geddes, economist at ABN-Amro in London. "We'll need more information before the market spikes out of these ranges."
Market attention will also be on next week's U.S. May payroll data, due on Friday. German unemployment is also expected on that day.
